items.prompt: A user who does not own an event type sends PUT /api/event-types/{id}. The handler returns Error.Validation("EventType.Forbidden", ...). What status comes back?
items.answer: 403, because ResultExtensions matches Forbidden in the error code
distractors: 400, because the error was built with the Error.Validation factory
404, so that the caller cannot confirm the event type exists
401, since the caller is not the owner of that resource
items.explanation: ResultExtensions picks the status from the error Code string only: EndsWith .NotFound is 404, Conflict/Taken/AlreadyCancelled is 409, Contains Forbidden is 403, else 400. The factory used does not matter. The handler found the event type (no NotFound), and the user is authenticated, so not 401.

items.prompt: A request sends X-Tenant-Slug: ghost, and no tenant has that slug. What does TenantResolutionMiddleware do?
items.answer: It sets nothing in Items and just passes the request on
distractors: It ends the request with a 404 that names the unknown tenant
It falls back to the Host subdomain and looks up that slug
It ends the request with a 400 before authentication runs
items.explanation: Lines 15-25: when the lookup returns null, the middleware simply skips setting Items and always calls next(context). It never short-circuits with a status, and the subdomain is only consulted when the header is absent (the ?? on line 13).

items.prompt: There is no X-Tenant-Slug header. For which Host value does TenantResolutionMiddleware look up a slug?
items.answer: acme.calendy.io, which yields the slug acme
distractors: calendy.io, whose first label calendy is used
localhost:5000, which yields the slug localhost
Any host at all; it always uses the first label
items.explanation: ExtractSubdomain splits Host.Host on dots and returns parts[0] only when there are at least three parts. calendy.io has two parts and localhost has one (Host.Host carries no port), so both give null and no lookup happens.

items.prompt: An anonymous visitor with no token calls GET api/schedules/available-slots, so no tenant_id claim exists. The handler runs currentTenant.TenantId!.Value. What happens?
items.answer: Value throws InvalidOperationException; the middleware sends 500
distractors: The ! operator turns the null into Guid.Empty, so no slot ever matches
The tenant id saved in HttpContext.Items is used as a fallback
The compiler refuses to build it, since TenantId is a Guid?
items.explanation: CurrentTenantService returns null when the claim is missing. The null-forgiving ! only silences the compiler's nullable warning; Nullable<Guid>.Value on null throws InvalidOperationException at run time, and ExceptionHandlingMiddleware turns any unhandled exception into a 500. Nothing reads HttpContext.Items here, and the code compiles. The endpoint is [AllowAnonymous], so this is a real bug for public visitors.

items.prompt: A caller's JWT expired two minutes ago. Program.cs sets ValidateLifetime = true and sets nothing else about timing. Is the token accepted?
items.answer: Yes, since the default five-minute ClockSkew still covers it
distractors: No, because ValidateLifetime rejects any token that is past its exp
No, since the default ClockSkew in ASP.NET Core is zero
Yes, because ValidateLifetime only checks the nbf claim
items.explanation: TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew defaults to 5 minutes and Program.cs does not change it, so a token up to five minutes past exp still validates. ValidateLifetime checks both nbf and exp, each with that skew; the default is not zero.

items.prompt: In one request, a handler adds one entity through eventTypeRepo and one through bookingRepo, then calls uow.SaveChangesAsync once. What happens?
items.answer: Both rows are saved in one transaction by the shared scoped context
distractors: Each repository saves its own entity in its own separate transaction
Only the entity added last is saved; the earlier Add is replaced
Nothing is saved until each repository calls SaveChanges itself
items.explanation: AddDbContext registers AppDbContext as scoped, and IUnitOfWork resolves to that same instance, so every repository in the request shares one change tracker. One SaveChangesAsync flushes all pending changes in one implicit transaction. Adds do not replace each other, and repositories have no save of their own.

items.prompt: Someone injects AppDbContext into a service registered with AddSingleton. What does the persistence guide warn will happen?
items.answer: The context outlives requests, piles up entities and goes stale
distractors: Each request still gets a fresh context, as EF scopes it itself
The container quietly upgrades the singleton to a scoped service
Only speed suffers; the tracked data stays current at all times
items.explanation: The guide calls it a captive dependency: the singleton holds the one context it got, so the context lives forever, accumulates tracked entities, and eventually throws or returns stale data. EF does not re-scope it, and the container never changes a registered lifetime.

items.prompt: UpdateEventTypeHandler loads an event type, changes its name and then calls eventTypes.Update(et). What UPDATE does SaveChangesAsync send?
items.answer: One that writes every mapped column, since Update marks all of them
distractors: One that writes only the name, since the entity was already tracked
None, because Update detaches the entity from the change tracker
An INSERT, because Update treats it as a new aggregate to be added
items.explanation: RepositoryBase.Update calls DbSet.Update, which sets the entity Modified with every property marked modified, so the UPDATE writes all columns. Without that call, snapshot change tracking would have written only the changed name. Update never detaches, and an entity with a set key is tracked as Modified, not Added.

items.prompt: A handler calls uow.SaveChangesAsync() after creating a User and again after creating a Schedule; the second save throws. What is left in the database?
items.answer: The User, because the first save had already committed by itself
distractors: Nothing, since EF rolls back every save made in the same request
The Schedule only, because the later save replaces the earlier one
Both, because the failing save is retried until it finally succeeds
items.explanation: Each SaveChangesAsync is its own implicit transaction, so the first commit is permanent even when the second fails; the guide calls two saves in one handler a review red flag. No request-wide transaction exists, the saves do not replace each other, and retry-on-failure covers only transient errors a limited number of times.

items.prompt: Today a booking is saved and BookingCreatedEvent is published through MediatR's IPublisher. What happens next?
items.answer: Nothing visible; MediatR finds no handler and simply returns
distractors: MediatR throws, because every notification must have a handler
A queued background job sends the confirmation email later on
The event is written to an outbox table for a retry later on
items.explanation: The repo has no INotificationHandler at all, and MediatR's Publish with zero handlers is a no-op. There is no Hangfire job and no outbox table; the guide lists both as future work.

items.prompt: Later, an email-sending handler for BookingCreatedEvent is added and it throws. What does the invitee's POST see, and what is stored?
items.answer: A 500 error, while the booking row has already been committed
distractors: A 201, as the email failure is logged and then swallowed
A 500 error, and EF rolls the booking row back as soon as it fails
A 201, and the email is retried by an outbox job later
items.explanation: AppDbContext awaits base.SaveChangesAsync first and publishes afterwards, so the row is committed before the handler runs; its exception propagates out of SaveChangesAsync and the middleware returns 500. Nothing swallows it, nothing rolls back a committed save, and there is no outbox.

items.prompt: SaveChangesAsync hits a transient Npgsql error. Going by DependencyInjection.cs, what happens?
items.answer: EF Core retries the operation up to three times before it fails
distractors: The error goes straight to the middleware and becomes a 500
Polly retries it with backoff until the request times out
The handler catches it and returns Error.Conflict instead
items.explanation: UseNpgsql is configured with EnableRetryOnFailure(3), an execution strategy that retries transient failures up to three times. The guide's gaps table says transient errors return 500, but its own note below the table, and the code, show the retry. No Polly policy or catch exists in the handlers.

items.prompt: An invitee posts the same cancellation token to api/bookings/cancel a second time. What status comes back?
distractors: 200, as cancelling a cancelled booking is a no-op
404, since a cancelled booking's token is retired
400, because the domain error falls to the default
items.explanation: Booking.Cancel returns Error.Conflict("Booking.AlreadyCancelled", ...) when the status is already Cancelled, and ResultExtensions maps codes containing AlreadyCancelled (and .Conflict) to 409. The token still resolves, the domain refuses rather than ignoring the call, and the code matches before the 400 default.

items.prompt: A signed-in user of tenant B calls GET /api/bookings/{id} with the id of a tenant A booking. What does the current code return?
items.answer: 200 with the booking, as GetBookingHandler checks no tenant
distractors: 404, because a global query filter hides the other tenant's rows
403, because the tenant_id claim does not match the stored row
401, since that token was issued for a different tenant entirely
items.explanation: GetBookingHandler loads by id through RepositoryBase.GetByIdAsync (FindAsync) and maps the result; nothing compares TenantId. That is RISK-001, an IDOR. No HasQueryFilter exists yet (the critique proposes one), and the token is valid, so neither 403 nor 401 happens.

items.front: NetCalendy's three validation layers: what each checks.
items.back: HTTP input (CreateBookingValidator): format such as valid email, future start, non-empty name. Domain invariants (Booking.Create): business rules such as start < end. Database (EF config + Postgres): unique cancellation token, FK constraints. They overlap on purpose: defense in depth.

items.front: The four reliability gaps in the side-effects guide, with their fixes.
items.back: No outbox for domain events (transactional outbox or Hangfire); transient save failures (Polly or EnableRetryOnFailure, which is already configured); no circuit breaker for future external calls (Polly); concurrent double-booking (unique partial index on host_id, start_time).

items.front: Owning NetCalendy for three months: the priority order.
items.back: 1) RISK-001 IDOR on GetById and RISK-005 broken public event-type read; 2) RISK-003 double-booking via unique partial index; 3) RISK-002 timezone validation (TimeZoneConverter); 4) RISK-004 outbox or Hangfire for event side effects; 5) RISK-006 rate limiting, global.json, UpdateEventType validator, EF global query filters.

items.front: Safe way to remove a column under rolling deployment.
items.back: Deploy 1: stop reading the column (remove it from the EF config). Deploy 2: add the migration that drops it. Two steps, so old instances never query a column that is gone.
